name: Narrative bias
statement: Narrative bias is the finding that a few single-case stories shift risk judgements away from the statistical base rate shown alongside them.
meaning: Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid define the target as 'the excessive influence of narrative information, exemplars, and testimonies, which we refer to as narrative bias'. The paradigm behind that sentence is fixed and narrow. A participant reads a statistic giving the rate of some adverse event, then reads a set of first-person reports of which a known share describe that event happening. If judgement tracked the statistic, the share would not matter. It does. Raising the share of reports describing the adverse event raises perceived risk and lowers stated willingness to accept the treatment. The claim is about how two samples of evidence get weighted, not about stories in general. Betsch and colleagues name Borgida and Nisbett's 1977 study as the classic case. A few brief personal accounts there had a stronger impact on students' course choices than mean course evaluations. That paper was not obtained for this entry, and the description of it here is the 2015 paper's. The same words carry two other meanings. Nassim Taleb's narrative fallacy, from chapter 6 of The Black Swan, is defined in his glossary as 'our need to fit a story or pattern to a series of connected or disconnected facts'. That is a claim about explanation, not about weighting evidence. Moore and colleagues use narrative bias for reporting spin. They define it as 'a tendency to interpret information as part of a larger story or pattern, regardless of whether the facts support the full narrative', and score it in the titles and abstracts of trials and reviews. Of the three, only the first has been tested as a claim about people, on the searches recorded below. The contest between a narrative message and a statistical one is a different question, and anecdotal evidence, entry 489, carries it. Confabulation, entry 42, covers the narrative-construction literature.

origin.who: Cornelia Betsch, Corina Ulshöfer, Frank Renkewitz and Tilmann Betsch
origin.note: The experiments that fixed the paradigm. Their abstract reports two studies in a simulated online bulletin board. Experiment 1 varied 1, 2 or 4 of 10 narratives reporting adverse events. Experiment 2 crossed a statistical risk of 20% or 40% against 2 or 4 of 10 narratives, and against the richness and the emotionality of the reports. It found a stronger influence of the number of narratives than of the statistic, and a stronger influence of emotional reports than of unemotional ones, while richness had no effect. The label narrative bias is not in that abstract. It appears in the group's later papers, and the 2015 follow-up states it as a definition. Taleb's narrative fallacy is a different claim, described above, and The Black Swan was published in 2007, four years before these experiments. The earliest use of narrative bias in the present sense located here is the 2013 paper by Betsch, Renkewitz and Haase. That search covered Europe PMC by exact phrase, which returned 76 records on 21 September 2026 with no earlier use in this sense, and Crossref by bibliographic query. No source claiming to coin either phrase was found.

evidence: The follow-up that carries the name was read in full. Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid ran two experiments. Experiment 1 was run on 290 students at the University of Erfurt, 24.5% male, mean age 22.16, SD 3.159; thirteen were excluded and 277 were analysed. The design was 2 x 2 x 3 between subjects. It crossed the statistical rate of vaccine adverse events, 5% or 40%, against the share of 20 first-person reports describing an adverse event, 1 or 8 of 20, which is the same 5% or 40%. Which of three measures came first was the third factor. The statistic appeared as a percentage and as a matrix of 100 elements. On a visual analog risk scale, answered first by 94 subjects, the reports outweighed the statistic: standardised beta = .43, p < .001 for the reports against beta = .29, p = .002 for the base rate. On a percent probability estimate, answered first by 89 subjects, the ranking reversed, beta = .81, p < .001 for the statistic against beta = .15, p = .02 for the reports. On a 7-point probability rating, answered first by the other 94, the statistic took beta = .56, p < .001 and the reports beta = .16, p = .07, which the authors report as not significant. They also report a negativity bias on the risk scale, where the reports raised perceived risk rather than lowering it, while the percent estimates moved symmetrically. Experiment 2 drew subjects from Amazon Mechanical Turk for US$1: 515 clicked through, 479 finished, and 464 were analysed. It held the statistic at 20% and set the share of adverse-event reports at 10%, 20% or 40%. Perceived risk again tracked the reports, beta = .38, p < .001, n = 168, while the percent estimate showed no significant effect, n = 181. Doubling the pool of reports from 10 to 20 while holding the share constant changed nothing. Subjects spent twice as long on 20 reports as on 10, 3 min 31 s against 1 min 46 s, F(1,337) = 60.96, p < .001. Three checks on the procedure left the effect standing. It was as strong when reading the reports was optional as when it was required, F(1,92) = 19.11, p < .001, partial eta squared = .17, and 78.2% of the 55 subjects offered the choice read them. It was unchanged when the statistic came after the reports instead of before, F(1,109) = 16.07, p < .001, partial eta squared = .13. Numeracy cut the bias on some measures and not others. In Experiment 2 the more numerate showed the weaker effect on perceived risk, beta = -.14, p = .05 for the interaction. In Experiment 1 subjective numeracy interacted with the reports on the percent estimate, beta = -.14, p = .02, and did nothing on the risk scale. Four other papers from the same group were read only as abstracts. Betsch, Ulshöfer, Renkewitz and Betsch report that the number of narratives influenced judgement more than the statistical risk did. Betsch, Renkewitz and Haase ran 458 participants through a simulated patient network, varying the reports at 1, 7 or 17 of 20 against summary statistics, narratives or both. They report that summary statistics had the smallest impact, narratives more, and both together the most, and that a disclaimer warning of the bias reduced the influence of the network. Haase, Betsch and Renkewitz gave 265 people 20 reports attributed either to an anti-vaccination website or to a neutral health forum, against a 20% statistic. They report a stable narrative bias unaffected by credibility cues, with the anti-vaccination attribution lowering perceived risk overall. Haase, Schmid and Betsch ran three online experiments with 564 subjects, varying the share of adverse-event reports at 5%, 20% and 35% against a 20% statistic. Risk perceptions and intentions moved in both directions. Neither likelihood of infection, severity of disease nor perceived susceptibility changed the size of the shift. Independent groups get less tidy results. Ubel, Jepson and Baron gave prospective jurors in Philadelphia County hypothetical figures of 50% benefiting from angioplasty and 75% from bypass surgery, together with written testimonials from hypothetical patients. In their first study 44% chose bypass when the mix of testimonials was proportionate to those figures and 30% when it was disproportionate, P = 0.002. In their second study the same contrast gave 37% against 34%, P = 0.59, and 58% of a group shown no testimonials at all chose bypass. Fagerlin, Wang and Ubel used the same angina scenario on prospective jurors at the Philadelphia County Courthouse and travellers at Detroit Metropolitan Airport, without saying in the abstract which group went to which study. The anecdotes moved choices when the statistics were in prose, 41% against 20% choosing bypass, chi-square = 14.40, P < 0.001. They did not when the statistics were reinforced with a pictograph and a quiz, 38% against 44%, chi-square = 1.08, P > 0.20. In their second study the quiz left the anecdotes' influence intact, 27% against 28%, chi-square < 1, P > 0.20, while the pictograph moved choices from 27% to 40%, chi-square = 6.44, P < 0.001. Obrecht, Chapman and Gelman report higher estimates of event frequency when individual cases arrived one at a time than when the same cases were summarised. A third study of theirs found subjects treating each data sample as one instance rather than weighting it by its size.

examples.tag: The leaflet with accounts printed under it
examples.text: A leaflet states that a side effect occurs in one case in a thousand and prints six patient accounts, two of them describing that effect. Readers rate the risk higher than readers given the same figure under six accounts that mention nothing.

examples.tag: Owner reports below the repair rate
examples.text: A page gives the annual breakdown rate for a boiler and then twenty owner reports, a handful describing a failure. The share of reports carrying the bad outcome moves the judgement, although the rate printed above them has not changed.

examples.tag: The question that asks for a number
examples.text: The same reader who marks the risk high on a sliding scale gives an answer close to the stated rate when the form asks for a percentage instead. Part of the effect belongs to how the question is put.

replication.headline: The effect holds across the Erfurt group's experiments and similar effects appear in independent work. It shrinks when the judgement is asked for as a percentage, it disappears when the statistic is drawn as a pictograph, and it failed in one of two studies by an independent team.
replication.detail: Betsch, Haase, Renkewitz and Schmid put the effect against two artefactual explanations and it survived both. It did not depend on whether the reports were read by choice or by instruction, or on their position relative to the statistic. It also did not depend on the absolute number of reports, only on their relative frequency. What it did depend on is the question asked. The same experiment gave beta = .43 for the reports on a visual analog risk scale and beta = .15 on a percent probability estimate, where the base rate took beta = .81. The other conditions come from the group's other papers, each read only as an abstract: source credibility in Haase, Betsch and Renkewitz, and disease risk in Haase, Schmid and Betsch, neither of which changed the bias. Independent teams split. Ubel, Jepson and Baron found testimonials moving treatment choice by 14 percentage points in one study, P = 0.002, and by 3 points in the next, P = 0.59. Fagerlin, Wang and Ubel reproduced the effect with statistics in prose, 41% against 20%, and removed it by adding a pictograph and a quiz, 38% against 44%. Both of those studies predate the Erfurt paradigm and use a different task, so they are neighbours rather than replications of it. Winterbottom, Bekker, Conner and Mooney reviewed 17 studies. In five of them narrative information influenced decision making more than no extra information or statistical information did. First-person narratives were twice as likely as third-person ones to produce an effect. No later experiment by the original group, and no direct repeat of their paradigm by anyone else, was located. That search covered Europe PMC by author and by the phrase, on 21 September 2026, and Crossref by bibliographic query. The honest summary is that the effect is steady in the paradigm that names it and conditional everywhere else.

study.cite: Betsch, C., Haase, N., Renkewitz, F., & Schmid, P. (2015). The narrative bias revisited: What drives the biasing influence of narrative information on risk perceptions? Judgment and Decision Making, 10(3), 241-264.

limits: No effect size is carried in the structured fields, because the studies report standardised regression coefficients, percentages and chi-squares, and putting a beta beside a percentage-point difference would suggest a comparison the papers do not support. The n recorded above is Experiment 2 of the 2015 paper, the sample analysed rather than the 479 who finished; Experiment 1 analysed 277 of 290. Only the 2015 paper was read in full, fetched twice from two hosts, the publisher's PDF at Cambridge University Press and the journal's own PDF at journal.sjdm.org, and every figure was checked against both. The 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2020 papers by the same group were read only as their abstracts at Europe PMC, as were those by Ubel, Fagerlin, Obrecht and Winterbottom. The sample sizes and percentages quoted from them are the ones their authors chose to put in an abstract. Two of those were chased further on 21 September 2026 and are still unread. Fagerlin, Wang and Ubel is listed as free at the publisher by Unpaywall and by OpenAlex, and the Sage PDF returns a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall or a price; no repository copy is listed. Obrecht, Chapman and Gelman is listed the same way, and the Springer PDF returns a client challenge of the same kind; the authors' pages at Rutgers and William Paterson list the paper without a file. Neither block is a subscription wall, and a reader with a browser may well get through. Five experiments in the core line come from one group at the University of Erfurt, and the sixth, Experiment 2 of the 2015 paper, is the same group on a United States online panel. Every study in that line uses a fictitious disease and a hypothetical vaccination, and the outcome is a stated intention rather than a vaccination. Borgida and Nisbett's 1977 study, named in the 2015 paper as the classic case, was not obtained; Unpaywall reports no open copy and Wiley returns a bot challenge. The search for tests of Taleb's narrative fallacy covered Crossref by bibliographic query and Europe PMC by exact phrase on 21 September 2026. Crossref returns no empirical study of it by that name, and the 25 Europe PMC records for the phrase are commentary, editorials and reviews rather than studies of human subjects. Freling and colleagues' meta-analysis of the anecdotal bias is the pooled comparison of narrative against statistical messages, and it belongs to anecdotal evidence, entry 489, which quotes its figures. It could not be reopened here. The repository copies at Texas Rio Grande Valley and at North Carolina at Greensboro both returned bot challenges on 21 September 2026, and the publisher's page at Elsevier returned 403. Its numbers are therefore left to that entry rather than restated from memory. Braddock and Dillard's 2016 meta-analysis of narrative persuasion was not obtained either. Unpaywall reports no open copy and Taylor and Francis returns a bot challenge, and no figure from it is quoted here. Allen and Preiss's 1997 meta-analysis appeared only in a search-engine summary and was left out for that reason.
misreadings: The first error is to read Taleb's narrative fallacy and the tested narrative bias as one idea. Taleb's is a claim about explanation, that people cannot look at a sequence of facts without weaving a story into it, and chapter 6 offers no experiment of his own. The tested bias is a claim about weighting, that a sample of cases pulls a judgement away from a base rate presented in the same session. The second error is inherited from Taleb's own retelling of the study he leans on. He describes an experiment in which 'the subjects were forecasting professionals' who judged the odds of a massive flood in America against an earthquake in California causing a flood. In Tversky and Kahneman's paper that item went to a sample of 245 undergraduates at the University of British Columbia in April 1982, half seeing each version. The wording is 'somewhere in North America in 1983'. The geometric means were 3.1% for the conjunction and 2.2% for the flood alone, p < .01 by a Mann-Whitney test. The forecasters were a separate group of 115 people at the Second International Congress on Forecasting in Istanbul in July 1982. They judged a different pair, about relations between the United States and the Soviet Union, at .47% against .14%. The third error is to take the bias as proof that stories beat numbers. Where the comparison is a narrative message against a statistical one, the pooled syntheses put the statistic ahead on average and the sign flips on severe, personal and medical topics; anecdotal evidence, entry 489, carries those figures. The fourth is to treat the effect as a fixed property of people rather than of the display. It shows up on a visual analog scale asking how risky something feels. It shrinks on the same page when the question asks for a percentage. Fagerlin and colleagues switched it off by drawing the statistic as a pictograph. The last is to assume every paper titled 'narrative bias' is about the same thing. Moore and colleagues use the term for spin in the titles and abstracts of clinical trials, which is a property of writing rather than of readers.
